title: Model Outline
text:
We build a stack of models that simulate the process of preference formation and an election in the electorate of the population of Aarhus. Once for the municipal election and once for the national election.
First, we will focus on the municipal election.

title: Survey Results
text:
The survey was conducted in the population of Aarhus, Denmark, and includes questions about beliefs, belief certainties, and preferences on five national topics: security, economics, welfare, immigration, and climate change. On Aarhus local topics, it has the ten most relevant questions from the Voting Advice Application (Kandidattest) for the municipal election.
Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggstats)
library(scales)
library(gt)
library(patchwork)
library(partycoloR)
library(glue)
data <- read_csv("SurveyData/survey_responses_ENG_TRANS.csv")

title: Survey Results
text:
1.2 Belief, Uncertainty, and Preference Distributions
Insights:

For all topics, beliefs are more skewed towards agreement than preferences.
Certainty about the beliefs is generally high.
Preferences have the typical pentamodal distribution spanning all possible opinions with peaks at the two extremes in the middle and two off-central moderate opinions (see Gestefeld et al. 2022). This maybe caused by some condensing around focal or socially emergent values.
Taking standard deviation (SD) as a measure of polarization, beliefs preferences are most polarized with Climate Change most and Immigration preferences least polarized. Beliefs are generally less polarized (partly a consequence of the positive bias) with Economic belief being most and Security belief being least polarized. On uncertainty there is the least variation in Mean and SD over all five topics.



Code
data_nat_long <- data |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(ends_with("_B"), ends_with("_P"), ends_with("_BCRT")),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Response"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Label = word(Variable, 1, sep = "_"),
    Type = word(Variable, 2, sep = "_") |>
      str_replace("BCRT", "Certainty") |>
      str_replace("B", "Belief") |>
      str_replace("P", "Preference")
  ) |>
  select(-Variable) |>
  left_join(nat_domains_questions, by = "Label")
data_nat_long_fractions <- data_nat_long |>
  count(Response, Label, Topic, Type, Preference_q, Belief_q) |>
  mutate(Fraction = n / sum(n), .by = c(Topic, Type))
data_nat_long_fractions |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Response, y = Fraction, fill = Fraction)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  facet_grid(Topic ~ Type)

title: Survey Results
text:
1.3 Belief-Preference Relation
Insights:

On economics and welfare the belief-preference relation is strongly positively correlated. (Who believes economic inequality is too high strongly tends to agree that the tax for the highest incomes must be raised; and who believes people who need public support do not always receive enough help tends to agree that the transfer income for the poorest cash assistance recipients must be increased.)
On security and climate change the belief-preference relation is moderately negatively correlated. (Who believes Denmark faces serious security threats is tends to disagree that Denmark spends too much money on supporting Ukraine; and who believes climate change poses an urgent threat to Denmark tends to disagree that nuclear power must be part of the energy supply.)
On immigration the belief-preference relation is essentially uncorrelated. (The belief that immigrants are not integrating well does not predict the preference for opening up more foreign labor non-European countries.)



Code
data_nat_belpref_fraction <- data_nat_long |>
  filter_out(Type == "Certainty") |>
  select(userId, Type, Topic, Response) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Type, values_from = Response) |>
  count(Belief, Preference, Topic) |>
  mutate(Fraction = n / sum(n), .by = Topic)

data_nat_belpref_fraction |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Belief, y = Preference)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Fraction, color = Fraction)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(weight = Fraction), formula = 'y ~ x') +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7) +
  scale_color_gradient(high = "darkgreen", low = "lightgray") +

title: Survey Results
text:
1.4 Belief Extremity and Certainty
Belief extremity is calculated as the absolute distance of the belief response from the neutral point (5).


Code
data_nat_extr <- data_nat_long |>
  filter_out(Type == "Preference") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Type, values_from = Response) |>
  mutate(Belief_Extremity = abs(5 - Belief), .by = Topic)
data_nat_extr_fraction <- data_nat_extr |>
  count(Belief_Extremity, Certainty, Topic) |>
  mutate(Fraction = n / sum(n), .by = Topic)


Insights:

Belief extremity and certainty are positively related for all topics in a very similar way. The overall correlation is 0.56.

The answering categories for the local preference questions were \(-2,-1,0,+1,+2\) as in the original Voting advice application.

    names_to = "Label",

  count(Response, Label, Preference_q) |>
  mutate(Fraction = n / sum(n), .by = Label)


Insights:

The distribution of preferences only sometimes show a pronounced neutral peak above 40%. Most notable on ALCL4 on making it cheaper to run businesses and ALCL8 on the stopping the expansion of Aarhus Harbor.
Rarely there are pronounced peaks at the two extremes. Only ALCL6 on more mosques and ALCL10 on the new football stadium shows a tri-modal structure with peaks at the two extremes and in the middle.
The most positive topics are ALCL5 (social mixing in schools) and ALCL7 (more parking space) with means above 0.5.
The most negative topic is ALCL3 asking for more tasks in public sectors to be solved by private companies.
The most polarized topic are ALCL6, ALCL9 and ALCL10 on mosques, car traffic reduction and the new football stadium.
Least polarized is ALCL4 on making it cheaper to run businesses.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text: The following steps are how data is used in the process of building and validating an agent-based model following Lorenz (2021). Figure 1 gives an overview of the process.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text:
1 Initialization
Setting up the foundational state of the model. The simulation environment is created and the initial values of its parameters are set. The agents are created and the initial states for their static and/or dynamic variables are set. Doing it data-driven means in the first place that the variables are analog to variables which are observable in the real world. This enables validation and calibration with empirical data. Data-driven initialization can also mean more specifically that the initial values of the variables are set based on empirical data. While this can be a starting point for a realistic simulation run, it goes againt the goal of having the model be able to reproduce the distribution of the variables as an emergent property of the model.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text:
2 Exploratory Data Analysis
Exploration of empirical data to understand the distribution of the variables and their relationships, and to identify stylized facts that the model should be able to reproduce. Done by visualizing, calculating standard summary statistics, and defining relevant targeted metrics.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text:
3 Validation
Data-driven validation is measuring a model’s ability to reproduce empirical stylized facts. This is also called assessing the replicative validity. Methods and metric can be similar as for macro-calibration (see below) but with a different focus. While calibration is model-internal parameter-tuning process to make it match data better, validation is a model-external assessment about its quality.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text:
4 Calibration
Adjusting free parameters and simulation procedures such the the model matches its real-world subject better. Data-driven micro-calibration means that parameters and simulation procedures have realisitic microlevel foundations. Data-driven phenomenological macro-calibration means that parameters and simulation procedures are adjusted to match the stylized facts as quantifies be macrolevel metrics. While the former is imporant for counter-factual scenario studies, the latter is important for building forecasting models. Ideally, both do not lead to strong deviations but are consistent with each other.
